title: The design argument: Paley, Hume, Darwin
note: Design arguments infer an intelligent cause from order in nature. Paley argued from biological contrivance: parts arranged for a purpose, like a watch's, imply a designer. Hume's Philo had already questioned the analogy and the kind of designer it supports; Darwin's natural selection offered a non-intelligent source of adaptation. Later versions shift to laws, molecules, or the cosmos.

read.title: The watch on the heath
text: Paley opens Natural Theology with a contrast. A stone found on a heath might have lain there forever. A watch found on the ground could not, because when we inspect it we see 'that its several parts are framed and put together for a purpose.' His argument can be set out:

(1) The watch's parts are arranged so that together they serve a purpose. (2) Such arrangement, in every case where we can check, comes from an intelligent maker. (3) Living things, such as the eye, show the same kind of arrangement, in greater degree. (4) Therefore living things also have an intelligent maker.
Paley anticipated several objections. A watch that sometimes runs badly still shows design. So does one whose maker we have never seen at work.

Hume's Philo had already pressed harder objections in the Dialogues of 1779. The universe is not very like a machine, so the analogy is weak; at best it supports some designer or designers, perhaps imperfect ones. Darwin then removed premise (2) for biology: natural selection, acting on variation over long ages, produces arrangement that serves survival without foresight.

Defenders reply in more than one way. Some argue that Paley's inference is not a weak analogy but an inference to the best explanation. Others, like Swinburne, move the argument from organisms to the laws of nature themselves, which natural selection presupposes and cannot explain.

q.q: Why can't the watch's presence be explained as the stone's is?
o: Its parts are framed together for a purpose
It is smaller than the stone

q.q: Which premise did Darwin's theory undercut for biology?
o: That such arrangement always comes from an intelligent maker

q.q: How does Swinburne's version escape the Darwinian objection?
o: It argues from the laws of nature, which selection presupposes
It argues from the age of the earth
